title: How Steve Jobs explained Apple's iTunes Music Store: owning the whole ecosystem
summary: In a 2003 launch-day interview, Jobs explains why the iTunes Music Store beats piracy and subscription services: a complete, integrated experience (store, jukebox, iPod) that is expensive and slow for rivals to copy. He frames Apple's job simply as making stuff, and credits trust with artists for landmark deals.

principles.text: Own the whole experience end to end so the product is a complete solution competitors can't piece together.
principles.quote: we've now built the first real complete ecosystem for the digital music age.

principles.text: Beat free alternatives by making the legitimate experience clearly better, not by lecturing.
principles.quote: the experience is so much better than Kazaa, I think a lot of people don't want to spend 15 minutes downloading a song and getting a less than perfect quality song

principles.text: Products that restrict users fail; give people broad rights to what they buy.
principles.quote: you can't put it on your MP3 player, you can't put it on multiple computers—it sucks!

principles.text: Reject fancy labels; the work is simply to make things and let people use them.
principles.quote: We make stuff, put it out there, and people use it.

principles.text: Compounding investments in infrastructure, software and hardware create a moat that is hard to copy.
principles.quote: to recreate this, it's tens of millions of dollars and years. That's why I don't think this is going to be so easy to copy.

principles.text: Win partners by being credible and artist-friendly, which earns trust to negotiate landmark deals.
principles.quote: they see Apple as the most creative of the technical companies, a very artist-friendly company, very credible.
